Modern humans have Neanderthals to thank for a common genetic variant that affects the occipital lobe.

A gene mutation inherited from Neanderthals may reduce the risk of schizophrenia by almost 10%, a new study has found.

The study found that Neanderthals passed on a common genetic variant affecting the occipital lobe, which is found at the back of the brain. The occipital lobe is home to the brain’s visual cortex and plays a role in vision, mental imagery and reading.

Neanderthals are thought to have had larger occipital lobes than modern humans. Yet modern people with the genetic variant have smaller occipital lobes — a reduction of about 0.85 cubic centimeters per copy, according to the study, which was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The variant lies near DAAM1, a protein-coding gene involved in brain development.

In people with two copies of the gene variant, it is also linked to a nearly 10% lower risk of schizophrenia, but the variant does not seem to affect intelligence or other major psychiatric disorders.

“This Neandertal-derived variant is linked to altered brain anatomy in present-day humans and lower schizophrenia risk while having little or no association with general cognitive ability,” wrote study authors and evolutionary geneticists Hugo Zeberg and Svante Pääbo

“These findings caution against equating the size of a brain region with cognitive abilities,” they added.

Zeberg, of the Karolinska Institutet in Sweden, and Pääbo, a 2022 Nobel Prize winner from the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Germany, have worked together for years to identify how Neanderthal genes affect human health today.

They previously found that a major Neanderthal-inherited gene cluster on chromosome 3 raises the risk of severe COVID-19. Subsequent research found the same variant protects against HIV.

Researchers are exploring how lifestyle choices affect the ageing brain.

With people living longer, tips on how to keep the mind sharp with age are everywhere. But not all of them are equally supported by scientific evidence.

Experts at the Society for Neuroscience’s annual meeting highlighted how lifestyle changes can help protect the brain against age-related decline — and where the science isn’t quite settled.

While the advice to eat well and exercise has been around for decades, Heather Snyder, senior vice president of medical and scientific relations at the Alzheimer’s Association, noted that the scientific understanding of how these behaviours influence the brain and support brain health is still evolving.

“By understanding the science, what we can do is better inform our recommendations, particularly for those individuals that are most at risk,” she said.

How does exercise benefit the brain?

Exercise has long been associated with better health, with benefits ranging from reduced cardiovascular risks to improved mental health.

But can physical activity also promote healthy brain ageing, and what biological mechanisms explain its effects on the brain?

“Exercise is a powerful non-pharmacological intervention that fosters and promotes brain health,” said Fernanda De Felice, a professor at the Center for Neurosciences Studies at Queen’s University in Canada.

Exercise can help preserve brain volume as we age, improve blood flow and influence inflammatory processes in the brain, De Felice added.

“When we think about the body and we think about physical exercise, we can think about our muscles exercising. And it makes sense, right? All the tissues and systems are here, close to our muscles. But how come exercise is actually good for the brain?”

The answer, De Felice explained, lies in communication between the muscles and the brain.

“The body can communicate with the brain,” she said. “Whenever we don't have a completely healthy body, the brain senses it. But if we stimulate the periphery to become fit, the brain also feels the impact.”

What type of exercise is best for brain health?

While the benefits of physical activity are well established, different types of exercise can have different effects on the body and brain.

According to De Felice, the most important thing is to be consistent and make physical activity a habit. The World Health Organization recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week for adults.

Aerobic exercise has been shown to have a positive impact on both physical and brain health. “It stimulates blood flow and opens up the blood-brain barrier and makes these good molecules reach the brain,” De Felice said.

Resistance training and high-intensity interval training (HIIT) can also improve muscle function and increase muscle mass, stimulating the production of molecules that have neuroprotective effects, she said.

“Even walking, like just a moderate walk, has been shown to be important,” De Felice noted.

While 10,000 steps a day is a commonly cited target, she said people can see health benefits at lower levels of physical activity, making it important for people to stay active regardless of how many steps they manage.

“I would say that any type of exercise, any level, anything that you can do, to try to keep active. And more important than the steps, I would say that consistency is key,” she added.

Can intermittent fasting protect the brain?

Physical activity is not the only lifestyle factor that can influence brain health. Diet also plays an important role, with researchers investigating how eating patterns affect the brain's ability to age healthily.

Some studies suggest that intermittent fasting may have benefits for brain health, potentially by reducing inflammation and oxidative stress. However, much of the evidence comes from animal studies, and although early findings are promising, fasting has not been proven to prevent cognitive decline or protect against Alzheimer's disease in humans.

Researchers are still investigating whether the effects observed in experimental studies translate into meaningful long-term benefits for people.

“Food scarcity has been a major driver of brain function,” said Mark Mattson, an adjunct professor of neuroscience at Johns Hopkins University, adding that evolution has equipped the brain and body with the ability to function well during periods of fasting.

Intermittent fasting refers to eating patterns that alternate periods of food intake with periods of fasting. One common approach involves fasting for 16 hours and restricting eating to an eight-hour window.

During prolonged fasting, the body uses up its glycogen stores and starts breaking down fat, which the liver converts into molecules called ketones. These provide an alternative energy source for the brain and may also help protect brain cells by reducing inflammation and oxidative stress, Mattson noted.

The potential benefits of intermittent fasting may also be linked to the way cells respond to metabolic stress, a mechanism that has similarities with the effects of exercise.

Mattson noted that exercise and intermittent fasting work in a similar way, they both challenge cells, prompting protective responses. Meanwhile, periods of rest and recovery allow them to repair, grow and adapt.

“Over periods of weeks, months and years, these intermittent exposures to mild metabolic stress or challenges improves general health, function and counteract aging and disease,” he added.

At the cellular level, this means that during challenging periods such as fasting or exercise, cells switch into a mode in which they conserve resources and become more resistant to stress, Mattson said. A 36-year-old man in Poland experienced rare, debilitating complications after a tattoo done with red ink.

A 36-year-old Polish man had a tattoo done with red pigment in the summer of 2020 – and his health quickly took a turn for the worse.

He experienced numerous complications, including erythroderma, alopecia, anhidrosis and acquired depigmentation (vitiligo), according to researchers from the Wroclaw Medical University.

Only after cutting out the skin with the red tattoo pigment did the autoimmune diseases begin to regress.

"No cases of such an extensive nature, involving multiple organ systems, have been recorded so far," the researchers said.

They emphasised that adverse reactions to pigments used in tattoos are being recognised more and more often, but serious, systemic complications remain rare and poorly understood.

Red tattoo ink is often the cause of hypersensitivity reactions that do not appear immediately after the tattoo is done.

Erythroderma, hair loss, vitiligo and complete lack of sweating

After the tattoo with red ink was done, the man developed a rare and previously undescribed group of complications.

The 36-year-old had the tattoo done on his forearm in the summer of 2020. Four months later he developed itchy lesions. Over the following months these turned into erythroderma, a peeling inflammation of the skin. In the years after getting the tattoo he also lost the ability to sweat, lost all body hair and developed vitiligo.

After months of ineffective treatment, patch tests were carried out, confirming hypersensitivity to components of the red ink. An allergy specialist advised him to have the inflamed parts of the tattoo surgically removed from his forearm. This procedure led to the resolution of the erythroderma, but did not improve his other symptoms. In addition, his vitiligo continued to progress.

In total, the man underwent eight surgeries. Only complete removal of the red ink combined with medication allowed his hair to grow back and halted the progression of vitiligo. Anhidrosis, meaning the absence of sweat secretion from the sweat glands, remained unchanged.

The man had Hashimoto thyroiditis, reported a greatly reduced tolerance for physical exertion and was unable to do any work because of the risk of heat stroke linked to his anhidrosis.

Researchers call for regulations

In their paper, the researchers stress that the link between allergic and autoimmune diseases and adverse reactions to tattoo ink shows the need to raise awareness and exercise caution, especially in people who are prone to such reactions.

"Perhaps introducing regulations on licensing tattoo artists and education on safe tattooing will help reduce the number of complications associated with tattoos," they recommend.

In 2022, the European Union introduced rules on the composition of tattoo inks to limit the use of hazardous chemical substances. However, appropriate regulations are still lacking in many countries.

In the case of the Polish man, it was not possible to analyse the chemical composition of the tattoo ink, because he did not obtain either a sample of the product or its packaging from the tattooist.

From carpet-weaving and pottery-making to metalwork and paper marbling, Türkiye has a rich history of craftsmanship. Different regions boast different skills, and a tour of the country reveals some of its most treasured cultural pastimes.

Türkiye’s place at the continental crossroads of the world made it a major vein for the lucrative Silk Road trade route, which ran through the heart of the country for nearly 1,500 years. As well as facilitating the exchange of goods between Asia and Europe, the Silk Road also bolstered Anatolia’s own offerings, helping an already flourishing economy of handicrafts and artisanal products to bloom. Different parts of Türkiye became known for their output: silk from Bursa, carpets from Kayseri, ceramics from İznik.

Today, many of these crafts are still practised, some for industry and some to preserve historic practices. Beyond the region’s famed ceramics and textiles, visitors can discover metalwork including coppersmithing, the art of ebru (paper marbling) and tezhip (illumination), oya lacework and jewellery making including mother-of-pearl inlay (sedef kakmacılığı). All of these crafts are listed on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

We delve into some of Türkiye’s most distinctive handicrafts, discover what makes them special and where best to experience them.

Ceramics and pottery

Spurred on by China’s porcelain exports in the 15th century, Türkiye established itself as a major player in the ceramics world. Moving away from their previously unglazed, simply-designed pieces, potters in the İznik region began producing gorgeously glazed blue and white plates, vases and tiles. The Kütahya region is also renowned for its exquisite 14th-century tiles and pottery.

As the craft evolved, designs became more intricate and expressive, with the 16th-century seeing the introduction of vibrant colours such as greens and reds, and the craft achieving such prominence enough to require regulation.

It wasn’t long before many of these striking creations adorned some of the most iconic buildings of the day: the Süleymaniye, Blue Mosque and Rüstem Pasha mosques in İstanbul and the mausoleums of Süleyman I, for example. Visitors can see replicas of these unique pieces in the city centre of İznik today, as well as in its museum, where they can also take part in workshops. The originals can be seen in a dedicated museum in Kütahya.

Kilims

Made almost entirely from wool, kilims are tightly-woven, traditional carpets which are ageless, having been a part of Anatolian culture since ancient times. They remain an important part of day-to-day Turkish life, and can be seen used most often as prayer rugs but also for simple interior decoration.

The patterns and motifs found on kilims are an integral part of their design and often hold deep meaning. Some of the most commonly featured are the elibelinde (a female figure symbolising fertility), boynuzlu (a ram’s horn symbolising heroism) and earrings (used as an indication that a woman in the family wants to get married). Wards against the evil eye are also popular.

These motifs take many forms, including a burdock plant, a five-fingered hand or a diamond divided into four sections. Some craftspeople would even weave an amulet thought to defend against evil into their kilim for additional protection. Kilims can be found widely across the country, though Konya (a city just south of Ankara) is known as the ‘cradle of carpet weaving’ and one of the best places to start shopping.

Silks

The Silk Road earned its nomenclature for a reason. At the time it began (around 130 BCE), silk was not only one of the most lucrative products on the continent, but a striking symbol of the trade between Asia and Europe. It wasn’t long before Türkiye began exploring its own sericulture production, a unique craftsmanship that has been listed as part of UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage.

La ville de Bursa, qui fut autrefois la première capitale de l’Empire ottoman sur la Route de la Soie et qui abrite le site classé au patrimoine mondial de l’UNESCO « Bursa et Cumalkzk : la naissance de l’Empire ottoman », est devenue un centre important pour le commerce et la production de la soie. Cependant, ce commerce ne s’est généralisé que plusieurs siècles plus tard, atteignant son apogée aux XVe et XVIe siècles, en partie grâce à Koza Han, un marché du XVe siècle dont le nom signifie « l’auberge du cocon de soie » et où l’on faisait le commerce des cocons eux-mêmes.

Travellers can visit the han today, which remains a major trading hub for silk in Türkiye and is replete not only with finished silk products such as scarves and shawls, but also raw cocoons.

Coppersmithing

Metalwork is one of the oldest crafts in Türkiye, and copper has historically been a particularly popular choice thanks to its malleability, wear resistance and prevalence in the region – copper ore has been mined in Anatolia for over 7,000 years. Being so old, coppersmithing techniques have varied across civilizations, with the Seljuks being particularly influential on its evolution.

Today the dövme– or hand-hammered – technique remains popular. After hammering the item into shape, intricate designs are then etched into the surface using either relief, openwork or scraping. Turkish coffee pots known as cezve are among the most commonly-made products, though plates, pans, cauldrons and other kitchen items – as well as decorative pieces – are still plentiful.

This ancient artform can be witnessed most easily in the southern city of Gaziantep. Walking into the Bakırcılar Çarşısı – or Coppersmith’s Bazaar – here, visitors will be overwhelmed by the sounds of hammering metal.

Verdict: In choosing Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond, has Amazon made an inspired casting choice or taken the safe bet?

The wait is finally over and we finally know the identity of the next James Bond.

After years of speculation following Daniel Craig's (very permanent) swansong in 2021's No Time To Die, the seventh 007 will be played by Robert Pattinson.

The British actor beat the likes of Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, Josh O'Connor, Nicholas Hoult and Jacob Elordi to the coveted role, and becomes arguably the most famous actor to be cast as Bond.

Verdict? It's simultaneously an inspired choice, a frustrating one, and a very safe bet.

First and foremost, Pattinson is a shrewd choice for 007 as there's a case to be made that he is one of the most interesting and versatile A-listers working today.

Since his breakthrough roles in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire and the Twilight franchise, the now-40-year-old British star has worked hard to prove he's more than just a teen heartthrob.

By choosing his projects and directors wisely, he's worked with some of the greats like David Cronenberg (Cosmopolis), James Gray (The Lost City of Z), Claire Denis (High Life), Robert Eggers (The Lighthouse), the Safdie brothers (Good Time), Bong Joon Ho (Mickey 17), Lynne Ramsay (Die My Love), and Christopher Nolan (Tenet, The Odyssey). All of these films have shown Pattinson to be a chameleonic and at times eccentric screen presence – and that he clearly has the acting chops to tackle any role.

Take 2026, which been a constant string of successes for Pattinson: The Drama, The Odyssey, Primetime... And we haven't even had Dune: Part Three yet – which is directed by none other than Denis Villeneuve, the director of the as-yet-untitled Bond 26.

With this impressive CV, there's every chance that Pattinson will make Bond his own and nail it.

That being said, we move on to the 'frustrating' part of his casting: Is Pattinson over-qualified for the role, and wouldn't it have been nice to give someone else get a chance? After all, the man is already a megastar and still the current Bruce Wayne / Batman, and The Batman Part II is still filming...

Can the actor playing the Dark Knight be James Bond as well? It feels like overkill, especially when you consider that the role of Bond has always made the star, not the other way around.

Sean Connery was a relative unknown before Bond; George Lazenby had never acted outside of a few ads; Roger Moore was a household name thanks to The Saint but hadn’t had a huge break on the big screen; Timothy Dalton had a great stage career but was not an established movie star; Pierce Brosnan was a Bond hopeful for years but remained best known for his role as Remington Steele in the TV show of the same name... Only Daniel Craig had some major big screen credentials with memorable roles in Road To Perdition, Layer Cake and Munich ... However, it was Casino Royale that made him a bona fide leading man.

By comparison, Pattinson is already a dependable and bankable leading man, an A-lister with still plenty to prove but one who has confirmed he's a huge box-office draw.

And with that comes the fact that Robert Pattinson is a very safe choice.

Bond 26 will be the first Bond adventure since Amazon took over the franchise from long-serving producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson, and they need to prove they're a safe pair of hands for this new era of Bond.

Under the old rule, Pattinson would not have been cast; a more up-and-coming actor would have been selected. What Pattinson’s casting tells us is that Amazon are not taking any risks: they want some bang for their buck, and are clearly aiming for the next Bond film to be - like Skyfall before it - a $1bn box-office success story. The odds are it will be, considering Pattinson's casting, as well as the choice of director.

Indeed, Denis Villeneuve is without a doubt the most exciting director to take on a Bond film. The Oscar-nominated filmmaker hasn't made a bad film yet: from Incendies to Prisoners, Sicario to Arrival, Blade Runner 2049 to adapting Frank Herbert's supposedly unfilmable Dune books and making them into this generation's Star Wars, this is a man who hasn't shown even the faintest hint of a stumble.

Add the fact that Bond 26 is being penned by Steven Knight, the writer behind Eastern Promises and Locke, and the creator / writer of Peaky Blinders, Taboo, SAS: Rogue Heroes and The Veil, and you've got what seems to be a surefire hit.

With expectations this sky-high, the next Bond movie will really have to deliver the goods, and with the role of Bond comes a fair amount of scrutiny – to say the least.

Measles cases are falling in Europe, but there are exceptions.

About 2,000 people have caught measles so far this year in the European Union and nearby countries, EU health data shows.

The region is on track to record far fewer measles cases in 2026 than in 2025, according to provisional data from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC). The agency has published reported cases in the EU, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway — the European Economic Area — through September 2026.

While figures for this year are likely to rise, the gap between 2025 and 2026 is wide. In the 12 months ending in September 2026, there were 2,325 measles cases, compared with 10,195 from the same period a year earlier, covering October 2024 to September 2025.

Even so, some countries are seeing sharp outbreaks this year.

Bulgaria and Italy have recorded around 600 measles cases each. In Italy, the number of cases has been steadily falling since April, when the country recorded 173 measles infections.

In Bulgaria, which saw just two cases in all of 2025, health officials say falsified immunisation records are playing a role in the outbreak. In one hard-hit region, about 60% of “vaccinated” children had no antibodies against measles, mumps or rubella, the three diseases covered by the vaccine.

No measles deaths have been reported in the EEA region as of September, ECDC data shows.

Measles is cropping up in other parts of Europe as well. In England, for example, there have been 1,055 confirmed measles cases as of 9 November. And Ukraine has reported 653 cases through September.

ECDC’s data is preliminary, and the year is not over. Still, 2026 is shaping up to be a calmer year for measles than other recent periods. There were 7,655 measles cases across the EEA from January to December 2025, and more than 35,000 cases in 2024.

The 2024 surge cost six countries their measles-free status in January, including Austria, Spain and the United Kingdom.

Despite the apparent overall decline this year, European health officials have warned that communities with low vaccination rates are at risk of outbreaks. Measles immunisation rates range from 68% in Romania to 99% in Hungary.

Measles is highly contagious, and at least 95% of a community must be vaccinated in order to prevent outbreaks. Two doses of the measles vaccine provide up to 97% protection against measles.

Most measles cases over the past year have been among unvaccinated people, according to the ECDC, which looked only at cases with known vaccination status. About 28% of cases were among children under 5, while 51% were aged 15 or older.

Off the coast of Kea lie three famous shipwrecks that attract sea lovers worldwide. The Greek island also offers about 81 kilometres of hiking paths in 12 main routes.

Kea is a particularly popular tourist destination. But it offers much more than sea, sun and good food.

Anyone with the right training can discover the three shipwrecks off the Greek island. The "Patris", the Britannic and the "Burdigala". The Britannic, sister ship to the Titanic, sank in November 1916 after hitting a German mine. It lies at a depth of around 120 metres.

Although its design had been significantly improved after the sinking of the Titanic, the ship went down in just 55 minutes. Thanks to appropriate lifesaving equipment, and the short distance from Kea, around 1,300 people on board were able to be rescued, while 30 lost their lives mainly because the lifeboats were launched too early and the engines continued to operate.

"Awe. The first feeling you get is really awe," Kea Divers owner Giannis Tzavelakos told Euronews. "The size is something extraordinary. I don't think you can easily find a wreck of this size that is accessible to divers. It is in very good condition. Even though at least 112 years have passed since it sank, everything is still in its place. It is essentially an underwater museum."

In 1975 Jacques-Yves Cousteau discovered the wreck of the Britannic. He and his team were the first to explore it a year later. After many years of effort, the Underwater Historical Site of Kea was created.

A pioneering themed park and underwater museum made up of three protected marine zones that surround the three emblematic wrecks.

"So at the moment when the divers reach the surface and take out their mouthpiece and mask, you see a sparkle in their eyes and a huge smile of satisfaction, because beyond everything else, for divers the Britannic is something like Everest," says Tzavelakos. "Every diver, at some point, dreams of managing to dive on the Britannic. Essentially it is the fulfilment of a life goal."

From the seabed to the mountain and the capital of Kea. Around 500 metres from the settlement stands the "Lion". It is an impressive 6th century BC sculpture carved into solid schist rock that looks out over the village.

The visitor who has come this far can continue their route and discover the island's paths. It is a network of marked routes of around 81 kilometres, with 12 main trails.

"Over the last year we have formed a group of friends who walk across the island and bring its paths back to life through our activities," says Anna Podogyrou, member of Kea's hiking group. "We carry out clean-ups, we try to include the springs we encounter on our routes. We cross the paths with respect and take care to keep them clean."

"The paths give the island a different tourism identity," says Podogyrou. "Almost all the paths run through the oak forest, which is of unique beauty and environmental importance. They end at beautiful beaches, connect the villages with one another and create a link between the past and the present."

The most important feature of the island's nature is the large forest of Valonia oak (Quercus macrolepis). Many argue that it is a remnant of the distant era when the Cyclades were covered with forests of deciduous trees.

However, it is also possible that it is the product of human intervention, since in the past the acorns were widely used in tanning. The oak forest of Tzia is the largest in the Cyclades region.

The short distance from Athens gives the island a significant advantage. It is ideal for a weekend, for a three day break, and in recent years even day hiking excursions are organised for those who want to discover the local trails.

Will subsidies for buying electric cars make mobility more sustainable in Portugal? The measure aims to help vulnerable families but raises doubts about running costs, reliance on private cars and EU policy towards Chinese competition.

The most vulnerable families and microenterprises in Portugal will be entitled to support for the purchase of electric cars. The announcement came at the beginning of November, during the debate on the State Budget for 2027, when the environment minister, Maria da Graça Carvalho, said that the government would support the purchase of more than 20,000 vehicles, intending to cover up to 80% of the value of the vehicle, up to a maximum of 15,000 euros.

The announcement raised questions from the outset. The details of the measure are still not fully known, also because final approval by the European Commission is still needed, since this support is included in the Social Climate Plan, with an estimated allocation of 104.5 million euros to subsidise the purchase of around 5,500 vehicles by the poorest families in a first phase, a target that could grow by about another thousand units during the negotiations still under way in Brussels.

The aim of the programme, and of this measure in particular, is "to combat energy poverty and promote more accessible and sustainable mobility", focusing on vulnerable families, "more exposed to the impacts of rising fossil fuel prices".

Thus, the government expects "to support the electrification of mobility of 5,500 vulnerable families" and "around 9,000 microenterprises".

According to the environment minister, the government chose to focus on vulnerable families because Portugal is one of the European countries where lower income households have more vehicles of their own. The average is around 20%, Maria da Graça Carvalho said, rising to 24% in rural areas. In the outskirts of large cities it is around 23%. These are generally older cars, with high carbon emissions, which the government wants to see replaced.

With regard to rural areas in particular, the minister stressed that people have a car "because they need one" and because "public transport does not solve problems in low-density regions".

Who is the support for?

According to the government, in total, 1.5 million households may be covered by this measure. First of all, it is aimed at beneficiaries of the social electricity tariff. There are about 750,000 families and they will have priority when applications are assessed. Then there are households with incomes below 80% of the national median income, that is up to 11,572 euros a year.

How much is the support worth?

The amount of funding has not yet been finalised and may range between 70% and 90%, but the Environment Ministry indicates that it should be 80% of the value of the vehicle. The amount of support can be increased by 1,000 euros if an old vehicle is handed in to be scrapped. There will also be support for buying chargers.

In addition, in the case of vulnerable families, VAT will not be borne by them, said (source in Portuguese) the environment minister in an interview with Rádio Observador. According to Maria da Graça Carvalho, VAT will be covered by other funding.

"It is not the programme that covers it, but we have other funding for VAT. And we do not require scrappage [of an old combustion car]. It is the only case in which we do not require scrappage. Why? Because in that way they [low-income families] can sell the car. So in this model between 2,000 and 3,000 euros are left for the family to pay. And therefore, if the family manages to sell the old car for 2,000, 3,000 euros, it can swap it for an electric car without having to put in its own funding [to make up the 20%]," she explained.

Families will be able to receive a maximum of 15,000 euros per vehicle. There will also be a cap on the price of vehicles that can be bought with the support. The programme will accept applications to buy electric vehicles costing up to 37,500 euros, new or used and less than five years old, because of battery life, as long as they are bought from a dealership, that is they cannot be bought from private sellers.

Payment will be made through a voucher system, as happens with the E-Lar scheme created by the government to replace gas cookers and water heaters, and there will be no need to pay money up front when buying the vehicle.

After buying the car with the support, can it be sold straight away?

Vehicles bought under this support scheme cannot be sold before three years have passed.

And what is planned for companies?

Maria da Graça Carvalho also said that the government will support, with 228 million euros, around 9,000 microenterprises, with a turnover of up to two million euros and fewer than 10 workers, in buying 13,700 electric vehicles, and companies will be able to apply for one or two cars. In this case the subsidy will cover up to 100%, excluding VAT.

Microenterprises will also be required to hand in one vehicle to be scrapped for each electric vehicle they buy. In addition, to qualify for support to buy electric cars they must also prove that fuel accounts for at least 5% of their expenditure.

And for public transport?

Electrification will also reach public transport. Co-financing worth 125.5 million euros is also planned for the purchase of 700 electric buses for low-density areas, intended for example for the mobility of workers and students and for transporting patients in these territories.

This funding includes buying charging infrastructure and shelters by the transport authorities.

Is electrifying private cars the best way to solve the problem?

Despite the environmental and social objectives of the measure, there are questions about how effective it will be and about the impact it may have on mobility patterns in Portugal.

António Alvarenga, a professor at Nova School of Business and Economics (Nova SBE), speaking to Euronews, believes that the incentive to buy electric vehicles may represent a positive step towards decarbonisation, but warns of some contradictory effects that need to be taken into account.

From an environmental point of view, the professor draws attention to the risk that the measure will encourage behaviour that produces a result opposite to what is intended. He gives as an example a family that until then used public transport or soft mobility options such as bicycles every day but, encouraged by state support, starts to use a private car. In that scenario, instead of reducing emissions, the incentive could help to increase them by replacing more sustainable ways of travel with a more polluting individual solution.

However the issue is not limited to vehicle emissions. Alvarenga believes that it is also necessary to assess the impact of the measure on road traffic volumes. By encouraging the purchase of electric cars, the government is promoting a change in the technology used, but not necessarily a reduction in the number of cars on the road.

On the contrary, by making it easier to buy a private car, the support may help to maintain or even increase dependence on individual transport, without resolving structural problems such as congestion, the use of public space and pressure on infrastructure.

For the professor, the energy transition should not focus exclusively on replacing combustion cars with electric vehicles. Reducing dependence on private cars remains one of the key challenges for a truly sustainable mobility policy.

Should the priority be buying cars or strengthening public transport?

Using public funds to subsidise the purchase of private cars also raises the question of investment priorities. In particular when there are other structural needs still to be addressed, such as strengthening public transport, rail and mobility solutions in suburban and rural areas.

Even so, António Alvarenga believes that, despite the limitations identified, "it is better to go ahead with this measure than not to go ahead with any".

The professor acknowledges that the incentive to buy electric vehicles does not solve Portugal's structural mobility problems, but believes that it can represent a positive step towards decarbonisation. In his view, the search for an ideal solution should not prevent the implementation of measures which, even if insufficient, may produce results.

How can the government ensure that the support leads to a real improvement in these families' mobility conditions?

Another challenge relates to the conditions needed to use an electric vehicle on a daily basis, especially for lower income families.

Even if they receive significant support when they buy the car, not all families have a garage or access to a private charging point, leaving them dependent on the public network.

On this point, Alvarenga draws attention to weaknesses in the current public charging system, which he considers not very transparent in terms of costs, with high prices and not very intuitive to use. The multiplicity of operators and the need to use different cards and apps make the network particularly complex for users.

Thus, although access to a car may be made easier by the subsidy, using it still represents a financial and logistical burden that may penalise precisely the families the measure is intended to support.

The risk that dealerships will absorb part of the subsidy

There are also questions about how public incentives may influence the sale price of electric vehicles.

António Alvarenga warns of the possibility that dealerships will adjust prices according to the amount made available by the state, absorbing part of the benefit that should reach consumers.

In that scenario, the subsidy may not translate into a real reduction in the financial effort required from families, instead benefiting sellers and manufacturers. This is therefore a risk that raises questions about how effective the measure is and about the monitoring mechanisms needed to ensure that public support really reaches its target groups.

Can electric cars made in China also benefit from the support?

Another issue raised by the Nova SBE professor concerns the origin of the vehicles that may benefit from Portuguese incentives.

Based on the criteria published by the government, only six electric cars are eligible for support for purchase by lower income families, and with the exception of the Citroën ë-C3 and the Renault Twingo they are all made in China.

The choice is even more limited when the 15,000 euro threshold is taken into account. Only three cars sold in Portugal fit within the price limit. Only the most affordable version of the Dacia Spring, priced at 13,740 euros, meets the threshold.

With the supplement associated with scrappage, which raises the threshold to 16,000 euros, the Leapmotor T03 at 15.284,5 euros and the Renault Twingo E-Tech at 15.845,3 euros may be added.

Of these three models, at least one is made in China, while the new Dacia Spring has recently started to be produced in Novo Mesto in Slovenia, on the same line as the Renault Twingo E-Tech. The first generation was made in China.

António Alvarenga accepts that public support may end up indirectly financing the purchase of cars made in China. This raises questions about the consistency between the environmental objectives of the measure and the European industrial policy, especially in a context of growing competition between European and Chinese manufacturers.

In this context the professor points to the example of France, which has adopted a different model for granting incentives to buy electric cars.

Since January 2024, the awarding of incentives for buying electric cars in France has excluded models made in China, even if they are from non-Chinese brands, because of environmental criteria and the carbon footprint associated with the manufacturing process and the energy used to make the vehicles.

The change came after the French authorities identified that around one third of the public incentives awarded were benefiting consumers who bought vehicles made in China.

The French programme represented an annual cost of around one billion euros and offered incentives of between 5,000 and 7,000 euros for buyers of electric cars. According to the French Finance Ministry, channelling a significant share of this support to cars made in China helped to increase imports and intensify competitive pressure on domestic manufacturers.

Europe urges households to be self-sufficient for at least the first three days of a crisis. Citizens should have enough food, water, and medicine, keep evacuation bags ready, and have emergency plans to face natural and human-induced disasters.

EU Commissioner for Preparedness, Crisis Management and Equality Hadja Lahbib presented the EU's new emergency preparedness guidelines on November 3.

The guidelines aim to make crisis preparedness part of everyday life, ensuring households can meet their basic needs for at least the first 72 hours when emergency services are stretched.

They cover everything from keeping emergency supplies and cooperating to making decisions under stress, teaching preparedness in early school education, and communicating risks.

"These guidelines have been developed with EU Member States and Union Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM) Participating States. This has been a collaborative process, including workshops and consultations", Lahbib explained.

The move comes after a wave of cyberattacks, drone attacks, sabotage of critical infrastructure, and natural disasters, which can cause disruptions to communications, transport, and energy networks, leaving entire communities paralysed.

Why now?

Threats take many forms, and some are close to home. Though the European Commission considers full-scale war unlikely, the EU's proximity to Ukraine poses a vulnerability. The bloc faces Russia's ongoing aggression in Ukraine, instability in the Middle East, and climate-driven floods and wildfires, alongside a surge in sabotage, drone incursions and cyberattacks.

The Commission adopted its Preparedness Union Strategy in March 2025 to shift Europe from reactive crisis management to proactive defence. But the guidelines gained importance in late 2026 following a string of hybrid incidents across Europe.

In late October, hackers remotely compromised internet-connected fridges across dozens of supermarkets in seven EU countries: Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Sweden, Finland, Estonia and Ireland. They switched cooling units to "defrost" mode, raising temperatures and ruining tonnes of food. A similar attack earlier in October hit roughly 700 supermarkets in France. French authorities attributed it to hackers from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Beginning on November 3, a week-long wave of anonymous bomb threats targeted at least 20 European airports, over 35 commercial flights and public broadcasters. Although all were hoaxes, they forced emergency landings, fighter jet escorts and terminal evacuations in Belgium, France, Italy, Ireland, Portugal and Denmark. Authorities in Ireland and France investigated possible foreign interference, concluding that the aim was to exhaust emergency resources and sow public panic.

Throughout 2026, EU officials also reported suspected sabotage and drone incursions near critical energy and transport networks, including the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport in August 2026.

How you should prepare

The new rules focus on ensuring households can meet their essential needs for at least the first three days, helping them manage until emergency aid is deployed. This includes having enough food, water, and cash, as well as practical skills such as cooking without electricity and first aid. Households should have emergency plans and evacuation bags containing important documents and medicines, ready to grab if evacuation becomes necessary.

The goal isn’t to create a single emergency kit for all of Europe, but to help national governments provide clear guidance on how to best prepare for emergencies.

"There is no one-size-fits-all emergency kit. Everyone should tailor their emergency kit to their individual needs, environment and geographical location. Everyone should use common sense and sound judgement when adapting what to include", Lahbib said.

The rules also encourage national authorities to use surveys to regularly assess whether households understand risks, have taken practical steps, and can meet essential needs.

Age-appropriate safety education should be embedded in pre-primary and primary schooling, helping children develop the knowledge and skills to recognise risks, follow warnings, call 112 and provide basic first aid. Preparedness can be taught through everyday teaching, play and routines, without imposing extra burdens on schools or causing fear or anxiety.

Preparedness must be inclusive and accessible so everyone can understand risks, access information, and act safely. Evacuations, transport, and shelter must account for different accessibility needs and involve people with disabilities in planning. First-aid responders should receive training to develop the knowledge and skills to communicate effectively, recognise specific support needs, and provide accessible assistance and protection.

Public authorities should share potential risks and threats in ways people can understand, trust, and act on, providing citizens with timely, reliable, and accessible information before, during, and after emergencies. This can include using appropriate communication channels tailored to local contexts or socio-demographic groups, addressing disinformation, and linking information to clear actions.

Why 72 hours?

The first three days after a crisis or disaster are crucial.

“Seventy-two hours is roughly how long authorities need to assess the damage, mobilise, and reach people who can’t help themselves […]. After day three, people should expect organised support to become available”, explained Ieva Birka, lead researcher at the University of Latvia Baltic Individual Crisis Preparedness Barometer.

This timeframe is drawn from a report titled “Better Together” (2024) by Sauli Niinistö, former President of the Republic of Finland, which calls on communities to be self-sufficient during various types of emergencies.

The first 72 hours are also when emergency services are under the greatest pressure, searching for survivors in collapsed buildings and restoring communications and energy networks. Self-sufficiency can ease the burden on emergency services, allowing them to “prioritise casualties and those most at risk”, Birka explained, but it “can’t replace professional help. No household preparedness measures can replace rescue, firefighting or trauma care”.

But this timeframe should be used as a rule of thumb, as pressure varies by crisis type. “In a flood or storm, demand peaks early with rescue and evacuation, then shifts to recovery. A cyberattack on critical infrastructure works differently. Pressure can build slowly and last a long time”, Birka told Euronews.

The guidelines recommend being self-sufficient for longer. “72 hours is a minimum, not a ceiling. In a long blackout, a hybrid campaign or a war, day four can look like day one”, Birka told Euronews.

Armed attacks are the crisis most likely to require long-term self-sufficiency because “infrastructure is targeted on purpose, the disruption lasts, and access for responders may be blocked”, she explained. Cyberattacks also call for long-term preparedness, as “failures cascade from one system to the next, and nobody can say when services will be restored. Natural disasters in Europe are usually local, so help can come from unaffected areas nearby.”

From recommendation to implementation

EU preparedness guidelines are non-binding, and implementation largely depends on national governments, creating differences across the bloc.

"The EU cannot guarantee that citizens are ‘equally prepared’. That is the responsibility of each Member State," Lahbib told Euronews.

She added that the guidelines could help bring countries closer together through practical advice, good practices and checklists to identify where preparedness needs strengthening.

Finland, Sweden, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania already have mature systems, such as Finland's 72 tuntia (72 hours) programme, which helped inspire the EU's. Sweden distributes crisis booklets to every household, while Estonia advises citizens to prepare for up to a week without outside help.

Germany, Poland, the Czech Republic and Romania were also pushed into action by their proximity to the war in Ukraine. Germany advises citizens to stock up on 10 days' worth of supplies, while the other three countries have introduced 72-hour preparedness programmes.

Lahbib said the EU developed its guidelines in consultation with member states, allowing governments to share experiences and learn from one another.

"Member States have been involved throughout. They have made valuable contributions," she said, highlighting the sharing of good practices.

However, countries like Belgium, France and other Western and Southern nations lag behind. According to the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS), public readiness is lower in these regions.

Preparedness also raises affordability concerns. Not every household can afford emergency supplies, potentially leaving low-income communities more exposed during crises.

"Being prepared does not have to be expensive. Simple steps can make a real difference," Lahbib told Euronews, citing family emergency plans and essentials such as food, water, medicines and a torch.

This is a European problem, as the bloc shares interconnected power grids, transport networks and supply chains. Uneven preparedness creates cross-border vulnerabilities, potentially straining the EU Civil Protection Mechanism if blackouts, cyberattacks or extreme weather hit multiple countries simultaneously.

Emergency services could become overwhelmed and draw on shared European reserves like rescEU. Panic buying in unprepared countries could also spread across the single market, triggering shortages in neighbouring regions.

Unprepared countries could also become weak links in the EU's wider strategy, allowing adversaries to exploit vulnerabilities and maximise disruption.

But preparedness is not just about governments and emergency services. It also depends on citizens supporting one another during crises.

"Preparedness is not just about what you have at home. Practical skills, previous experience, strong social networks and support within communities can make a real difference," Lahbib told Euronews.

"This is not about replacing the authorities’ role," she added. "It is about building a culture of community and shared responsibility: we are all in this together, and we all have a role to play in helping ourselves and each other to the best of our capacities when a crisis hits."

HSBC says every G7 member will need Italian-style primary surpluses to stabilise debt, as Rome borrows more cheaply than Paris ahead of an election-year budget.

In September 1992, Italy was the cautionary tale of European finance. The lira was forced out of the European exchange rate mechanism, the currency slumped, and Rome had to convince investors that it could still pay its bills.

What followed was more than three decades of belt-tightening that Italians still argue about. Year after year, the state collected more in revenue than it spent, before counting the interest on its debt.

Economists call this a primary surplus. Italy has posted one in 28 of the 34 years since 1992, according to International Monetary Fund data.

Now one of the world's largest banks says the rest of the Group of Seven will have to do the same.

"Every member of the G7 will have to follow Italy," Janet Henry, global chief economist at HSBC, said in a note last week titled "Turning Italian?".

Her argument rests on simple arithmetic. When the interest rate a government pays on its debt stays above the growth rate of its economy, debt keeps rising as a share of output, unless the government spends less than it collects before interest.

With borrowing costs high across advanced economies, Henry expects that gap to persist.

A lesson Italy learned the hard way

Henry was careful not to turn Italy into a model pupil.

"Italy is no poster child: the debt stock is still high, but it has run a persistent primary surplus for many years, initially forced by a severe currency and debt crisis in 1992," she said.

The difference, in her view, is that Rome has kept up the effort for decades, while the others have barely started.

"Unlike Italy, none of the others are on track for a prolonged adjustment," Henry said.

Only countries that have felt some pressure from bond markets, such as the United Kingdom, have tried to tackle their deficits over the past year, she added.

Not even the United States escapes the problem. Henry cited an estimate by the director of the Congressional Budget Office, the US fiscal watchdog, that stabilising American debt through growth alone would require nominal growth of 7-8% a year at current rates.

She also warned that the easy exits are closed. Governments cannot slash spending the way Greece and Portugal did after the eurozone crisis, and productivity gains from artificial intelligence may not easily turn into higher tax revenue.

"Difficult political choices lie ahead," she said.

Only one G7 country spends less than it collects

The latest IMF figures show how lonely Italy's position is.

According to the Fund's October Fiscal Monitor, Italy is on course for a primary surplus of 1% of GDP this year, rising to 1.2% in 2027. It is the only G7 economy expected to run one.

France is heading for a primary deficit of 2.9% of GDP this year. Germany, long the eurozone's fiscal disciplinarian, is projected to run a primary deficit of 3.4% as it ramps up spending on defence and infrastructure.

The United States is expected to run a primary deficit of 4.9%, Canada 2.6%, and Japan and the UK about 1.2% each.

How far the others would have to travel is a matter of debate. Writing in the IMF's Finance & Development magazine in March, economist Zsolt Darvas estimated that France and the United States would each need a primary surplus of 1.3% of GDP to stabilise their debt, and the UK 1.8%.

For France, that would mean improving its budget by more than four percentage points of GDP. Darvas noted that Paris has hit the required level only six times in five decades.

Italy, to be clear, still carries the heavier load. The IMF expects its public debt to reach 137.9% of GDP this year, the highest in the eurozone and above Greece's 136%. France stands at 118.5%.

Bond markets have already changed their minds

Investors appear to have reached a similar conclusion to HSBC.

On Monday at 13:26 CET, Italy's 10-year government bond yielded 4.43%, while France's equivalent OAT yielded 4.93%.

That means Rome is borrowing for a decade at half a percentage point less than Paris. On Friday, the gap closed at 50 basis points, the widest in Italy's favour since at least 1999, according to TradingView data.

The reversal has been fast. At the start of 2025, Italy paid 34 basis points more than France. The two lines crossed in September 2025, and the gap has kept widening since.

Italy now also borrows more cheaply than the UK, where the 10-year gilt yields 5.35%, and the United States, where the 10-year Treasury yields 5.12%.

Against Germany, the eurozone's benchmark, the BTP-Bund spread stands at 106 basis points. The spread measures the extra return investors demand to hold Italian rather than German debt. France's equivalent gap is 156 basis points, more than double the 71 basis points it started the year at.

Italy has not been immune to this year's sell-off. Its spread has widened from about 60 basis points in late February, as the war in the Middle East pushed up energy prices, inflation expectations and borrowing costs across Europe.

Claus Vistesen and Melanie Debono, economists at Pantheon Macroeconomics, expect that move to unwind.

"We think the BTP-Bund spread will fall next year, more than reversing its widening this year," they said in a note on Thursday. "We look for a BTP-Bund spread of 20bp by mid-2027, from just over 100bp at the moment."

Part of their reasoning is France. They argue that its more serious fiscal problems, along with uncertainty around next year's presidential election, will keep investors turning to Italian bonds.

Even then, cheaper relative borrowing would not make Italy's debt cheap. "Yields will stay high, at just above 3%, keeping the Italian government's debt costs elevated for now," they said.

An election-year budget tests the model

The bigger test for Italy may come from Rome itself.

Giorgia Meloni's government approved its 2027 budget on 28 October, a package worth about €26 billion that is now going through Parliament.

Much of it is tax relief.

For 2027 only, the 33% income tax band would be extended to earnings of up to €55,000, from €50,000.

Young private-sector workers born after 1997 and earning up to €28,000 would pay a flat 1% tax on pay rises of up to €2,500. Raises from renewed labour contracts would be taxed at a flat 5% for workers earning up to €33,000.

The self-employed would be able to stay in the flat-tax regime with turnover of up to €100,000, up from €85,000.

Car tax would be permanently scrapped for one insured car of up to 80 kilowatts per owner, and mothers of two or more children earning up to €40,000 would receive a tax-free €100 a month.

To pay for part of it, banks and insurers face a three-point rise in corporate income tax for two years, energy companies a higher regional business tax, and the tax on financial transactions would double to 0.8%.

Italy's Court of Auditors, which oversees public spending, told lawmakers on 9 November that many of the tax breaks expire at the end of 2027 and that about 70% of the funding will not be repeated, leaving the bill to the next Parliament.

The government's own fiscal plan, published in October, sees the deficit at 2.9% of GDP this year, rising to 3.4% in 2027 once extra defence and energy spending allowed under EU rules is included.

Debt is projected to edge up to 138.5% of GDP next year.

A vote too close to call

The budget lands as Italy heads towards a general election due by autumn 2027, with growing talk in Rome of an earlier vote in the spring.

The latest SWG poll for broadcaster La7, published on 9 November, put the centre-left opposition on 44.9% and Meloni's centre-right coalition on 44%, a gap within the margin of error.

Meloni's Brothers of Italy remained the largest single party on 28.9%, while 29% of respondents did not state a preference.

Pantheon's base case is that the governing coalition survives the vote, which it sees as a further reason for the spread to stay tight through 2027.

In 1992, Italy had no choice but to tighten its belt. Thirty-four years later, the rest of the G7 is being told to do the same, just as Italy is being tempted to loosen its own.

From Xylella to avocados, Salento is testing a new type of agriculture. But the spread of the bacterium worries Europe, and the tropical turn raises a key challenge: water availability.

Hass, Bacon and Fuerte: in Salento the new stars of the countryside have exotic names. Between Calimera and Vernole, in the province of Lecce, these avocado varieties are now an increasingly tangible presence, to the point that in mid November the harvest swung into full gear. They are no longer just an agricultural curiosity but a conversion gamble for Apulian farms seeking an alternative after the mass destruction of olive trees caused by Xylella fastidiosa.

That gamble, however, also has a downside. Avocado needs a lot of water precisely during the hottest summers, in a region already grappling with drought and aquifers under pressure.

The transformation is visible at the Tommasi farm, where the first plants were put in the ground in 2017. Almost ten years on, each tree produces between 70 and 100 fruits, for an estimated yield of around 10 quintals per hectare. Last April another 700 trees were planted.

And while Salento changes its crops, Xylella continues to pose a threat to European agriculture, turning a crisis that began in Apulia into a problem for the entire Mediterranean.

Xylella, a threat that no longer concerns only Apulia

The story of Salento’s avocado in fact starts with that of the lost olive trees. In October 2013 Xylella fastidiosa was detected for the first time in the European Union, in Apulia. It is a bacterium that colonises the xylem, the tissue through which water and nutrients circulate, progressively compromising the way the plant functions. In olive trees it can cause rapid desiccation and, in the most serious cases, the death of the tree.

Since then the disease has reshaped vast areas of Apulia’s agricultural landscape. And it has not remained confined to Italy: over the years it has also been found in France, Spain and Portugal. The crops affected include not only olive trees but also almond trees, citrus, vines and various ornamental plants.

The scale of the problem is confirmed by scientific research. In the latest update of its host plant database, published in 2025, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) recorded 727 plant species in which the presence of Xylella has been reported. For 463 of these there is stronger scientific evidence, based on specific detection criteria. This does not mean that all are equally vulnerable or that every subspecies of the bacterium can infect them: its ability to cause disease depends on the combination of bacterial variety, host plant and environmental conditions.

In 2026 new warning signs also emerged in Italy. In Calabria, in the territory of Taurianova in the province of Reggio Calabria, seven olive trees tested positive for the pauca subspecies. It is the first outbreak in the region. In Basilicata, meanwhile, the multiplex subspecies was detected on an almond tree in the Matera area. Emergency plant health measures and eradication operations have been put in place in both territories.

The spread of the bacterium makes surveillance an issue that goes beyond regional and national borders. For Europe, protecting agricultural production also means preventing a local outbreak from becoming a problem for entire supply chains.

The potential bill for European agriculture

How much could an uncontrolled spread of Xylella cost? An assessment published in November 2025 by the Joint Research Centre of the European Commission (JRC), together with EFSA, confirmed the bacterium as one of the main plant health threats for the Union.

In a large-scale spread scenario, annual production losses could reach 7.1 billion euro, with more than 540,000 jobs at risk. This is a simulation of potential impact, not a tally of damage that has already occurred.

The figure shows clearly why Xylella is not just an Apulian issue. Olive growing, almond production, citrus and winegrowing are important economic activities in several European countries. Loss of output would also have consequences for processing companies, distribution and all the businesses linked to agricultural value chains.

The European Union has therefore introduced specific rules to combat the bacterium. Xylella is classified as a quarantine pest organism and Implementing Regulation 2020/1201 lays down obligations for surveillance, delimitation of outbreaks and removal of infected plants.

When the bacterium is found in a new territory, the general rule is eradication: infected areas and buffer zones are established, with checks and plant removals as set out in the legislation. Where the disease is already widely established and elimination is no longer considered realistic, as in some parts of Apulia, containment measures are applied. Annual surveys are also carried out in the member states, and European co-financing is available for surveillance and control activities.

Prevention, however, does not bring back the lost olive trees. And this is where the search for new crops comes in.

Avocado, mango and papaya: the new face of southern farmland

For farmers who have lost a large part of their olive heritage, diversifying can mean avoiding abandoning their land and building new sources of income.

According to calculations by the Department of Soil, Plant and Food Sciences at the University of Bari, in Apulian areas affected by Xylella there are 23,885 hectares of olive groves potentially suitable for avocado cultivation. Land in Apulia devoted to tropical crops is already thought to total 4,000 hectares.

This is not just a business choice. Rising temperatures are changing the conditions in which traditional crops grow and creating opportunities for species that just a few decades ago would have been difficult to cultivate in these areas. Avocado, mango and papaya are among the clearest examples.

Climate data confirm the speed of change. According to Coldiretti Puglia’s processing of ERA5-Land data from Copernicus, in the first ten months of 2026 the Italian temperature anomaly reached +2.11 degrees compared with the 1991-2020 average. It is the highest value in the national data series for the January-October period.

But higher temperatures do not automatically mean better farming conditions. A crop may find a thermally favourable environment and still be unsuitable because of its water use, soil quality or vulnerability to extreme events.

Avocado: thrives in the heat but is thirsty

This is the main critical point of Salento’s conversion. Avocado is a subtropical species that requires a significant water supply, especially in the summer months. Olive trees, by contrast, are Mediterranean plants able to withstand prolonged periods of drought, thanks to physiological adaptations to the environmental conditions of the region.

The root system of the avocado is concentrated mainly in the upper layers of the soil, making the plant particularly dependent on available moisture. Agronomic estimates indicate water use that can reach 136-220 litres per day for an adult tree in summer, with lower values in spring.

The fruit’s water footprint is also significant. According to calculations by the Water Footprint Network by Mekonnen and Hoekstra, producing one kilogram of avocado requires on average 1,981 litres of water, taking into account rainwater, water used for irrigation and the water needed to dilute pollutants.

Naturally, not all litres have the same weight: rainwater and water drawn from aquifers and watercourses are different resources. It is therefore important to distinguish between the overall water footprint and actual irrigation water use.

For Salento, however, the problem remains concrete. Avocado is also sensitive to water salinity and poorly draining soils. These are particularly problematic characteristics in an area where underground reserves are under pressure and seawater intrusion is a documented risk.

A reprieve from drought is not enough

Apulia formally ended on 30 June 2026 its state of emergency over water shortages, after abundant rainfall in the previous winter and spring. But the end of the emergency does not equate to solving the problem.

Data from the ANBI Observatory updated at the beginning of October showed that the four artificial reservoirs in the Capitanata area contained 98.12 million cubic metres of water, less than 30 per cent of their total authorised capacity of 331.9 million.

In Salento, moreover, agricultural supply depends to a significant extent on underground resources. Hydrogeological surveys by Ispra have long documented falling aquifer levels and seawater intrusion, which can compromise the quality of available water.

The risk is that the expansion of crops with high water requirements will increase pressure on wells, fuelling competition between agricultural activities and household use. This difficulty is not confined to Apulia: water management has become one of the central issues for the future of Mediterranean agriculture, which is increasingly exposed to dry spells and irregular rainfall.

A new agriculture, but not at any price

Salento’s avocado shows that agricultural conversion can open up opportunities even in territories hit by a devastating plant health crisis. But it is not a universal solution. The trees take years to come into production, they require specific investments and they remain exposed to winter cold snaps, which can damage plantations.

The challenge, therefore, is to choose crops not only on the basis of new temperatures but also of actual water availability, soil quality and the ability to withstand extreme weather events.

There was one climate disaster a day on average in 2025 – and both rich and poor countries were badly affected.

The report, which does not account for the current ‘godzilla’ El Niño, shows how fossil fuel-driven warming is making extreme weather more deadly and more economically damaging.

Spain, France, Italy and Romania were in the top 20 most affected countries worldwide in 2025, with further extreme weather this year showing it was not a one-off event.

Almost a million lives lost to extreme weather in the last 30 years

In 2025, 367 extreme weather events were recorded worldwide, according to the Climate Risk Index (CRI) 2027. They caused nearly 35,000 deaths (it’s very likely the actual number is much higher than this as heat-related deaths are severely

underreported in poorer countries), affected more than 100 million people, and caused direct economic losses of more than US$158 billion (€143 billion).

Looking back over the last 30 years, 900,000 people lost their lives to extreme weather events and they resulted in direct economic losses totaling more than US$4.7 trillion (€4.2 trillion) – almost equivalent to Germany’s current GDP.

Between 1996 and now, the period the study looked at, rich countries, like Spain, France and Italy, have become much more vulnerable to deadly weather. The report’s authors say these countries should take the CRI results as a warning of the risks they face of frequent events, or rare but extraordinary extreme events: “The human losses and economic costs of climate-related extreme weather events will continue to rise unless there is a sizeable shift in mitigation ambition and financial support.”

In 2025, Jamaica, Sri Lanka and Spain were the most affected countries, followed by Thailand, the Philippines and Pakistan.

Why was Spain the third worst country for extreme weather in 2025?

Spain was hit by seven extreme weather events in 2025, with hundreds more that were devastating for local communities but not classed as extreme.

Spain’s deadliest event was a heatwave which spanned April to September and saw temperatures hit 46°C. It claimed 3,900 lives officially but is likely to have contributed to many more deaths. At the time, 2025 was Spain’s hottest summer ever, on average 2.1°C warmer than the 1991-2020 average, but it has now been surpassed by 2026.

Heatwaves kill people because high temperatures, especially when combined with humidity, impair the body’s ability to cool itself. This increases the risks of cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, kidney failure, diabetes complications and mental health impacts. Health impacts are highly unequal – older people, children and those living in inadequate housing are more likely to die.

2025 was Spain’s worst wildfire season in three decades

A particularly dry spring in western Spain, followed by the heatwave wiping out any remaining moisture in dense, dry vegetation, led to 2025 being Spain’s worst wildfire season in three decades.

The European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS) estimated that 382,607 hectares burned – about 1.5 times the size of Luxembourg.

Fires raged across Galicia, Asturias, Castilla y León and Extremadura. These regions, with the exception of Extremadura, are among the most depopulated in the country. Depopulation impacts forest upkeep. Traditional practices like extensive livestock grazing, which once naturally cleaned up the forest during the winter and spring, have largely disappeared. Fire brigades across the affected autonomous communities have repeatedly warned about the lack of forest management and limited resources.

The costliest event was Storm Alice, which caused US$100 million (€91m) in economic losses and affected more than 1,000 people. Alice triggered a weather event called a cold drop (Depresión Aislada en Niveles Altos), with rains leading to flooding.

Why heatwaves are such bad news for people – and the economy

Heatwaves were by far the deadliest type of extreme weather events in 2025, accounting for almost 70 per cent of all deaths.

Italy was the worst hit, with 6,710 deaths during a summer that reached 45.7°C, followed by 3,893 in Spain. In Germany, a heatwave reaching 38.3°C in July and August was the only extreme weather event registered in 2025. Nevertheless, it led to more than 2,400 fatalities.

Heatwaves are very bad news for the economy. In Germany, each day above 30°C is estimated to cause €124 million in economic losses, while globally output per hour generally declines by around USD$1.3 (€1.20) per worker for each additional degree between 30°C and 35°C.

Rising temperatures lower productivity and increase accidents and sick leave. Physically demanding jobs like construction are worst affected – with countries like Italy often having to ban outdoor work during the hottest hours of the day. Less output lowers tax revenues, while heat-related healthcare costs increase.

For informal workers, like fruit pickers or market traders, their earnings can fall by around 40 per cent during heatwaves, potentially pushing them into debt or having to take their children out of school.

Heatwaves can also disrupt infrastructure, as seen in Europe this year when nuclear power plants in France, Romania and Hungary had to shut down because there wasn’t enough water to keep them cool. Low river levels can also disrupt transport and increase costs for affected companies.

What are the solutions to reduce extreme weather?

Negotiators at COP31 could turn things around for all of us, with experts saying they must agree to transition away from fossil fuels. According to the UN, fossil fuels – coal, oil and gas – are by far the largest contributor to global climate change, accounting for around 68 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions and nearly 90 per cent of all carbon dioxide emissions. Extreme weather has become more extreme, frequent and deadly as emissions have risen.

Europe has been making good strides in the transition away from fossil fuels and to clean, renewable energy sources like wind and solar power. Many homeowners have got onboard by installing heat pumps in their homes. Policymakers need to direct more money away from fossil fuels and towards renewables.

When it comes to reducing deaths during heatwaves, cities that focus on reducing the urban heat island effect perform better. More trees and green space and less polluting vehicles are two of the keys to cooler cities. Milan, one of Europe’s most polluted cities, recently won a global prize for its plans to plant four million new trees and shrubs, helping to purify its smog-cloaked streets.

Ordinary citizens are also key in pressuring governments to take the climate crisis seriously and take real action. In the UK the National Emergency Briefing, a film that delivers the facts on how climate change threatens every part of our lives, has been shown thousands of times at free screenings around the country. Other European countries are now planning to make similar films about their countries.
