The glaring exclusion of High Representative Kaja Kallas from the Ukraine-Russia peace talks has raised uncomfortable questions about the relevance of her job. Defiant but isolated, Kallas stands by her words.

Since taking on the job as the European Union's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas has dealt with her fair share of setbacks, rebuffs and snubs.

But this one particularly stung.

Last week, Kallas flew to Dublin to attend an informal summit of leaders and make a forceful pitch to become the special European envoy for the ongoing negotiations to end Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

She framed her argument to leaders as self-evident: you chose me for this.

"In June 2024, there was a decision by the leaders (on) who is representing (the EU) when it comes to security and foreign policy. And it was the discussion that in these five years there is going to be a negotiation with the Russians," she said, referring to the division of top jobs at the start of the legislature.

"If the leaders want to change that agreement, of course, they may, because it is the leaders' decision, but I think we should focus our energy actually on the substance."

But leaders were unmoved and dismissed her pitch outright. According to people familiar with the closed-door discussions, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni argued that Kallas lacked the institutional weight and discouraged her candidacy.

The summit concluded with an expanded joint European team for the negotiations with a grand total of seven representatives. None of them was Kallas.

Adding insult to injury, the EU seat is shared by the European Council and the European Commission, with senior officials from the cabinets of presidents António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen, respectively. The European External Action Service (EEAS), the institution that Kallas oversees, is out of the picture.

Asked about her absence, neither Costa nor von der Leyen spoke in her favour.

Snubbed and pushed aside, Kallas now stares down a political reality in which she, the High Representative, whom the treaties task with conducting the EU's common foreign and security policy, is excluded from the most consequential diplomatic process the continent has lived through since the end of the Cold War.

It is a contradiction so glaring and profound that it challenges the very essence of her job.

Some in Brussels believe what happened in Dublin is the natural consequence of the missteps and gaffes that have made Kallas an increasingly divisive – and increasingly isolated – figure in the big-power city.

Kallas has ruffled feathers by going off script on sensitive matters, such as China and Israel, and putting forward initiatives with little or no prior consultation with capitals, including a defence expert group whose launch was cancelled last minute in September after pushback from Italy, France and others.

The displeasure has fuelled calls to reform. Germany, for instance, has proposed to place Kallas under von der Leyen's supervision, mimicking the top-down hierarchy in national governments between a prime minister and a foreign minister.

A senior diplomat pointed out that Kallas spent this year opposing direct talks with Russia, only to then pitch herself as the special envoy to deal with Moscow.

"If she actually talked to people and consulted with them, she would have known where the dynamics would lead to," the diplomat said. "Now, events have overtaken her."

"On the merits she is not wrong," they admitted. "Nothing will come of these talks anyway. There's no way Russia will engage constructively."

A second diplomat was equally critical and said Kallas had been very "clumsy" in her intervention in Dublin, where she declared "Russians don't want me" as envoy.

This diplomat believes that Kallas still retains the way of working she had when she was Estonian prime minister. Back then, her outspoken, hawkish views made her a political star in Europe. In her current role, they can easily backfire.

"It was not the right approach. She put herself in a difficult position. She still has in mind the fact that she was prime minister, and forgets that her role is simply to coordinate the positions of the foreign affairs ministers," the diplomat said.

"Her job is to find the lowest common denominator among member states."

Doomed to fail

The High Representative's pitch was doomed to fail for reasons that go beyond personalities, management style and political background.

Russia's war on Ukraine has become the be-all, end-all subject on the political agenda. Defence, security, trade, energy, finance, technology, sanctions and accession are all at stake in Ukraine. Billions have been provided in budget, military and humanitarian aid. How the war ends is set to define Europe for generations to come.

This has compelled leaders to be extraordinarily involved in the conflict, with countless visits to Kyiv and high-profile meetings. The decision by the leaders of France and the UK to launch the Coalition of the Willing best encapsulates the personal commitment.

But their commitment has come to the detriment of their foreign ministers and eaten away at their portfolios. More often than not, foreign ministers find themselves bickering and haggling without making decisions, which are ultimately made by leaders.

In fact, for the peace talks, leaders have relied on their national security advisors, who are part of their tight-knit cabinet. Even US President Donald Trump has left the task on two hand-picked envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, rather than on Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who, compared to Witkoff and Kushner, is harder on Russia.

Kallas, whose title is equivalent to Rubio, has suffered a similar fate.

Earlier this year, Kallas promoted a list of maximalist demands that Europeans should press Russia to fulfil as part of the negotiations.

Though the document was confidential, the High Representative quoted it so many times, including in Dublin last week, that she effectively made it public. While foreign ministers debated the document at length, leaders never acknowledged it and proceeded with their deliberations unconcerned by its existence.

"The reality is that no foreign minister has an obvious leading role here. Not because foreign ministers are irrelevant, but because the decisions at stake go far beyond traditional foreign policy," a third diplomat said.

"This is, quite literally, a matter for heads of state and government. They are the ones who can ensure political coherence across different areas and ultimately take responsibility for the commitments involved."

A fourth diplomat put it more succinctly, saying Europe should focus its energy on establishing a "consistent, unified position" for the negotiations rather than getting caught up in "unproductive discussions" of names.

Admittedly, the demise of the High Representative is a story that has been written many times in the past and never proven correct – or at least not its entirety.

The prevailing opinion blames the byzantine architecture of the EU treaties, which envisions a high-ranking figure bound by the principle of unanimity and deprived of enforcement powers, as the root cause of the problem.

Still, most diplomats agree that the Estonian's way of working is an aggravating factor. The lack of backing from the Commission, where she serves as vice president, and member states, whose views she is meant to represent, leaves her vulnerable to attacks. When backlash erupts, she is left to fend for herself.

Outside Brussels, however, Kallas remains popular and her no-nonsense takes on Russia are frequently praised and go viral online. The fact that the Kremlin openly detests her is used by her defenders to argue she is doing a great job.

Asked by Euronews if she regretted pitching herself as special envoy so forcefully, Kallas remained defiant.

"I stand by my words and I'm ready to do this job," she said, calling on leaders to uphold the EU treaties the same way they uphold the rule of law.

But she added: "It's also some kind of relief that we don't take about who any more.'

A massive European genome bank could pave the way for medicines tailored to each patient's DNA, faster diagnosis of rare diseases and new ways of prevention. Here's how it works.

Could a medicine one day be designed on the basis of the genetic characteristics of the person who is going to take it?

Could doctors know in advance which patients are more likely to respond to a treatment or to develop side effects?

And could the genetic causes of diseases that are currently hard to diagnose be identified more easily?

Personalised medicine is no longer just a distant scientific vision. Some of its applications are already used in clinical practice, while wider deployment requires much more knowledge of the human genome.

The Genome of Europe programme is one of the largest European population genomics projects. In total, 49 partners from 27 European countries are working together to create a shared reference base of at least 100,000 human genomes, which will reflect the genetic diversity of European populations.

The programme has a budget of €45 million, of which €20 million come from the European Commission through the Digital Europe programme. The project officially started in the autumn of 2024 and is scheduled to run for 3.5 years.

Cyprus is taking part in this effort through the Centre of Excellence for Biobanking and Biomedical Research biobank.cy at the University of Cyprus. Its contribution includes sequencing the whole genome of at least 310 Cypriot volunteers, feeding into the European reference base.

Why Europe needs a genetic map

Human DNA is, to a large extent, shared by all of us. However, small genetic differences are important for understanding inheritance, predisposition to certain diseases and, in specific cases, how people respond to medicines.

These differences are not distributed in the same way across all populations. This means that a genetic database built mainly from specific population groups may not adequately capture the genetic diversity of others.

Genome of Europe aims to close this gap by creating a representative European dataset that can be used as a reference point for future research.

"Populations, such as that of Cyprus, have their own specific characteristics," explained Katerina Strati, an associate professor in the biological sciences department at the University of Cyprus.

She told Euronews that understanding the genome at the local level is essential, because the relevant information cannot simply be inferred from research in other populations.

For scientists, a reference genome acts as a yardstick. It allows them to examine the genetic variants they identify in a person and to assess how common or rare they are in the population to which that person belongs.

Cyprus maps its own DNA

Mapping the Cypriot genome in its current form began in 2019, Strati explains. The aim is to create a genetic reference background for the country’s population, which will support medical research and molecular diagnosis.

Under the Cypriot Human Genome Project (CYPROME), more than 1,000 exomes from Cypriot volunteers have already been analysed. The exome is the part of the genome that includes the protein-coding regions of genes. Its analysis differs from sequencing the whole genome, which examines a much larger section of DNA.

Apostolos Malatras, a senior bioinformatician at the Centre of Excellence biobank.cy, explained that creating a reference genome allows researchers to compare genetic findings against a common background.

We will help make it much easier to design medicines and, of course, to use them: if a person has difficulty using a specific medicine, we will create a specialised medicine for that person

Today, biobank.cy holds more than 123,000 biological samples, involves 12,257 volunteers and is active in 14 research programmes, according to the figures published on its website.

The samples do not correspond one to one to genomes or participants. A volunteer can provide more than one sample, and DNA sequencing is a separate process.

Studies carried out at the Cyprus Biobank focus on hereditary kidney diseases, heart conditions and other illnesses. Its research programmes also include efforts to develop preclinical models for rare kidney diseases such as Alport syndrome.

Mariel Voutounou, a project manager at the Centre of Excellence, described the search for a treatment as a long and demanding marathon.

"When a doctor or scientist is interested in starting research into a condition, we say that they are starting a time-consuming marathon. And that is because it takes a great deal of time and effort to collect all these data and samples," Voutounou said. "Someone who has a whole biobank and this wealth of information in their toolbox, we say that their starting line is 10 kilometres ahead of everyone else."

Who protects patients’ DNA?

DNA contains highly sensitive information, not only about a person’s health but also about their biological relatives. How is it ensured that the genetic data of thousands of volunteers will not be used without their knowledge or consent?

The Cyprus Biobank operates with the approval of the National Bioethics Committee of Cyprus and in accordance with the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). As Malatras explains, biobank.cy applies multiple layers of technical and organisational security, with restricted access to personal data.

Dr Georgia Charalambidou, who is responsible for ethical, legal and social issues (ELSI) and education at the centre, explained that protection begins even before the first sample is collected.

"When a volunteer, an individual, comes here to the centre, the first thing we do is to provide them with sufficient information," Charalambidou said. "We try to make sure that they have understood it. We give them time to process it, to ask us questions and of course a consent form is always signed, in which all their rights are recorded."

Participation remains voluntary even after signing. "We always explain that they can withdraw their consent at any time, without any impact," Charalambidou stressed, clarifying that in the case of patients this decision does not affect their treatment or their relationship with their treating doctor.

The centre has also carried out a survey involving around 569 Cypriots, examining their views on genetic tests and taking part in genetic research.

According to Charalambidou, most participants were positive towards genetic research but want transparency and information about how their data are used. At the same time, they are interested in being able to receive results from the studies in which they take part.

"They want to know how we handle their data, what results exist. They also want to get something back," she said.

She noted that those who had been in contact with patients with diagnosed conditions were more positive about receiving genetic results back from specialist doctors. This finding, she added, highlights the need for better public information on genetic research.

Data work together without travelling

How can scientists in different countries use genetic data without putting their security at risk?

This is what the European Genomic Data Infrastructure (GDI) programme aims to ensure. It works alongside Genome of Europe, creating infrastructure for the secure interconnection of genetic data.

As Malatras explained, researchers will be able to carry out analyses on the systems where the data are stored, without the files themselves needing to be transferred from country to country.

This cooperation is particularly important for rare diseases, as it allows genetic findings from different populations to be compared.

Precision medicine is already used in some treatments, especially in oncology. However, the development of medicines tailored to the genetic characteristics of each patient remains a long-term prospect.

This is also the ambition behind the European collaboration: that the knowledge now being gathered from the DNA of thousands of volunteers will help deliver better diagnoses, more effective prevention and treatments tailored to patients’ needs.

Serviciile de informații susțin că Iranul dezvoltă planuri de a viza înalți oficiali ai Administrației Trump prin detonarea unor așa-numite bombe murdare sau a unor arme chimice la Washington. Totuși, conform surselor citate de CNN, oficialii americani nu sunt siguri că Iranul poate sau că va încerca să pună în aplicare un astfel de complot.

Sursele susțin că iranienii încearcă, de fapt. să-și ofere cât mai multe opțiuni și că informațiile obținute nu indică un atac iminent. Însă complotul descoperit de serviciile de informații americane este foarte specific și include locații și ținte, au declarat două dintre surse, și a declanșat o serie de planuri de contingență din partea SUA.

Într-un comunicat, purtătoarea de cuvânt a Casei Albe, Lauren Bis, a declarat că SUA ”monitorizează toate amenințările potențiale, dar în acest moment nu există amenințări credibile la adresa patriei”. Oficialii americani, însă, consideră că complotul iranian este un semnal al unei dorințe alarmante de escaladare din partea Teheranului, care se confruntă cu o presiune intensă din partea atacurilor militare americane și a unei blocade economice dure, despre care înalți oficiali ai administrației au spus că ”devastează” țara. Informațiile descoperite arată că Teheranul planifică acum activ potențiale atacuri pe teritoriul SUA, potrivit surselor, chiar dacă nu există încă dovezi că au decis să meargă mai departe. ”Dacă au de fapt personalul necesar pentru a executa atacurile este o chestiune de dezbatere”, a declarat una dintre surse.

Sursele au avertizat că Statele Unite sunt incredibil de vulnerabile la un atac cu arme neconvenționale. Bombele murdare – care ambalează materiale radioactive într-o bombă convențională – sunt relativ ușor de asamblat. Iranul nu ar trebui neapărat să introducă ilegal în țară oameni antrenați, ci ar trebui doar să convingă o persoană care locuiește deja în Statele Unite să comită atacul, scrie CNN.

Serviciile de informații americane au interceptat comunicații iraniene conform cărora Teheranul ar fi ascuns materiale pentru fabricarea bombelor în Statele Unite, potrivit uneia dintre surse. Oficialii sunt împărțiți în ceea ce privește credibilitatea acestor informații, dar, în general, cred că ar fi foarte ușor și chiar probabil ca Iranul să fi pre-poziționat deja materiale nucleare sau agenți chimici care ar putea fi aplicați pe o bombă convențională.

”Oricât de poroasă a fost granița noastră timp de aproape zece ani, ar fi fost extrem de ușor să introducă agenți în interiorul țării” care ar putea achiziționa și plasa componente ale bombei, a declarat una dintre sursele apropiate informațiilor. Mulți oficiali din domeniul securității naționale presupun că materialele nucleare pre-poziționate se află deja în SUA de ani, dacă nu de decenii, a spus o altă sursă. Cu alte cuvinte, capacitatea Iranului de a lansa acest tip de atac nu a crescut, a spus o altă sursă. Ceea ce s-a schimbat este motivația iraniană.
